query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing a portion of heavy Hf with a lightweight element such as aluminum in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the overall density without sacrificing its high strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent room‐ and elevated‐temperature strength.
generation.intervention: Substitute a controlled fraction of Hf (e.g., ~40% of the Hf content) with Al to create an alloy of approximate composition Al0.4Hf0.6MoTaTiZr.
generation.conditions: As‐cast state with subsequent standard processing, tested under quasi-static compressive and tensile loading over the temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase (or uniformly precipitated) BCC (or related solid-solution) microstructure similar to the original alloy, with possible minor ordered features from Al addition that help sustain solid solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s low atomic mass lowers the overall alloy density while its incorporation into the matrix introduces slight lattice distortions that can maintain or even enhance solid-solution and precipitation strengthening. This intervention is expected to offset the loss of some Hf contribution while preserving phase stability and high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a significantly reduced density (directionally lower than 10.21 g/cm³) while retaining comparable yield strength and ductility at both room temperature and near 1000 °C compared to the fully Hf-containing composition.
generation.baseline: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and proven high mechanical performance at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Performance evaluation should focus on the as-cast alloy under conditions ranging from room temperature up to ~1000 °C under quasi-static mechanical loading; microstructural integrity (i.e. phase stability) must be maintained across this temperature interval.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal level of Hf substitution with Al is not fully determined; there is some uncertainty regarding how much Al can be added without introducing detrimental phases or adversely affecting ductility and high-temperature stability. Fine-tuning the balance between density reduction and strength retention will require iterative experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys by arc melting: one the baseline equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr and the other with partial substitution of Hf with Al (target composition Al0.4Hf0.6MoTaTiZr). Conduct identical homogenization heat treatments for both. Characterize the phase structure via X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy. Then perform mechanical testing (compression and tensile tests) at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C. Measure the densities via Archimedes’ method.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate strength at room temperature and ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-substituted alloy exhibits either a density reduction that is not statistically significant or a degradation in yield strength, ductility, or phase stability (e.g., formation of detrimental phases or significant microstructural inhomogeneity) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High entropy alloys (HEAs), which include multiple principal elements, have attracted substantial research attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties, such as high fracture toughness, hardness, fatigue and corrosion resistances, yield strength, ductility and thermal stability,,,. In many applications, HEAs can significantly outperform traditional and super-alloys, especially at low and high temperatures,. Recently, the design of lightweight HEAs (with a density lower than 5 g/cc) has become one of the hottest research topics in metallurgy. In view of the outstanding performance of HEAs, the lightweight HEAs may have superior performance than traditional lightweight materials such as Al, Mg, and Ti alloys, with a large number of potential industry applications. Yet the chemical and compositional design space of HEAs is exceptionally vast, which makes the use of the traditional experimental methods for HEA screening an overwhelming task. Thus, an efficient, accurate strategy is required for the design of lightweight HEAs for specific applications,. Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
